title: Diabetes Diagnostics and Thyroid Function: HbA1c, OGTT, TSH, and Free T4
summary: The laboratory criteria for diagnosing diabetes and prediabetes (fasting plasma glucose, oral glucose tolerance test, HbA1c, random glucose), the strengths and interferences of HbA1c, and the logic of thyroid function testing with TSH and free T4, including common assay interferences such as biotin.
objectives: State the established diagnostic thresholds for diabetes and prediabetes and their required confirmation.
Explain what HbA1c measures and list conditions that falsely raise or lower it.
Describe the protocol and interpretation of the oral glucose tolerance test, including gestational diabetes screening.
Use TSH and free T4 together to classify thyroid dysfunction and recognize assay interference from biotin and binding protein changes.

highYield: Diabetes is diagnosed by any of: fasting plasma glucose at or above 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L), 2-hour OGTT glucose at or above 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L), HbA1c at or above 6.5% (48 mmol/mol IFCC), or random plasma glucose at or above 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms; asymptomatic patients require repeat confirmation.
HbA1c reflects average glycemia over roughly the preceding 2-3 months, weighted toward recent weeks; it is standardized through NGSP/IFCC but affected by red cell lifespan and hemoglobin variants.
TSH is the first-line test for suspected primary thyroid dysfunction; free T4 interprets it (high TSH with low free T4 = primary hypothyroidism; low TSH with high free T4 = thyrotoxicosis).
High-dose biotin can cause falsely low TSH and falsely high free T4 on common competitive immunoassays, mimicking thyrotoxicosis; always ask about supplements.
All diagnostic thresholds and reference intervals are method- and guideline-dependent; confirm abnormal results per accepted criteria and verify intervals with your local laboratory.

deepStudy.introduction: Endocrine testing is quantitative interpretation at its purest: small numerical thresholds carry diagnostic weight, so preanalytics, assay standardization, and confounders dominate the teaching. For diabetes, four diagnostic routes exist (fasting glucose, OGTT, HbA1c, random glucose with symptoms), each with strengths and failure modes. For the thyroid, the pituitary-thyroid feedback loop gives a two-test logic (TSH plus free T4) that classifies most patients, while assay interferences create classic exam traps. This lesson emphasizes the criteria, the confirmatory rules, and the interferents.

sections.heading: Glucose homeostasis and the diagnostic criteria for diabetes
sections.body: Plasma glucose is defended by insulin and counter-regulatory hormones; diabetes mellitus represents chronic hyperglycemia from impaired secretion, action, or both. The established diagnostic criteria (from widely accepted diabetes associations) define diabetes as any one of: fasting plasma glucose at or above 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) after at least 8 hours of fasting; a 2-hour plasma glucose at or above 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) during a 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test; HbA1c at or above 6.5% (48 mmol/mol, IFCC); or a random plasma glucose at or above 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) in a patient with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia. In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia with symptoms, a second abnormal test on a separate day is required for confirmation. Prediabetes is defined by intermediate values (for example fasting glucose 100-125 mg/dL or 5.6-6.9 mmol/L, 2-hour OGTT 140-199 mg/dL or 7.8-11.0 mmol/L, or HbA1c 5.7-6.4%), and these thresholds vary somewhat among guideline bodies; gestational diabetes has its own protocols. Specimen handling matters: glucose falls in unseparated blood as cells glycolyze, so fluoride or rapid centrifugation is used; the laboratory must verify intervals against its own method.

sections.heading: HbA1c: what it measures and what distorts it
sections.body: HbA1c is the fraction of hemoglobin with glucose attached to the beta-chain N-terminus (glycated hemoglobin). Because red cells circulate for roughly 100-120 days, HbA1c reflects average glycemia over the preceding 2-3 months, weighted toward the most recent weeks; it does not capture day-to-day variability or hypoglycemia. Assays are standardized through the NGSP and IFCC reference systems so that results are comparable across methods, but interferences remain. Anything that shortens red cell survival (hemolysis, blood loss, recent transfusion, splenomegaly) lowers HbA1c independently of glucose; iron deficiency can raise it; conditions with altered hemoglobin (HbS, HbC, HbE, HbF elevations) can interfere with some assay methods, so method choice matters in hemoglobinopathy-prevalent populations. Chronic kidney disease, pregnancy, and certain medications also complicate interpretation. When HbA1c is unreliable, glucose-based tests (fasting glucose, OGTT) or alternative markers such as fructosamine or glycated albumin (reflecting shorter windows) can be used; these too have method-specific reference intervals. Serial HbA1c trends guide therapy, with treatment targets individualized clinically.

sections.heading: The oral glucose tolerance test and gestational diabetes
sections.body: The OGTT challenges the system directly: after an overnight fast and a baseline glucose sample, the patient drinks a standardized 75-gram glucose load (100-gram load in the classic three-step gestational protocol), and plasma glucose is measured at fixed intervals, classically 2 hours (with intermediate sampling in diagnostic protocols). Preparation is strict: adequate carbohydrate intake for several days beforehand, no smoking or strenuous activity during the test, and accurate timing. The 2-hour value of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or above diagnoses diabetes; 140-199 mg/dL (7.8-11.0 mmol/L) indicates impaired glucose tolerance. Gestational diabetes screening commonly uses a 50-gram nonfasting glucose challenge test followed, if abnormal, by a 100-gram three-step diagnostic test interpreted with Carpenter-Coustan criteria, or a one-step 75-gram protocol per IADPSG/WHO; which protocol applies is set by local obstetric policy. The OGTT is more sensitive than fasting glucose but less convenient and more variable; preanalytical factors (acute illness, stress, steroids, bed rest) can invalidate results and testing should be deferred during acute illness.

sections.heading: Thyroid function testing: TSH, free T4, and interference
sections.body: The hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis produces a log-linear relationship: small falls in free T4 cause large rises in TSH, making TSH the most sensitive first-line test for primary thyroid dysfunction in ambulatory patients. The two-test logic: high TSH with low free T4 = primary hypothyroidism (Hashimoto thyroiditis is common); low TSH with high free T4 = thyrotoxicosis (Graves disease, toxic nodular goiter, thyroiditis); low TSH with low free T4 suggests central (secondary/tertiary) hypothyroidism and requires pituitary evaluation; discordant results raise assay interference or nonthyroidal illness. Total T4 and total T3 depend on thyroxine-binding globulin: estrogen, pregnancy, and hepatic disease raise TBG (high total hormones, euthyroid), while androgens, nephrotic syndrome, and severe illness lower it; free hormone assays avoid most but not all of these issues, and direct analog free T4 immunoassays can be biased in severe illness or with binding protein abnormalities, with equilibrium dialysis as the reference method. Two classic interference stories: high-dose biotin (vitamin B7) in competitive immunoassays causes falsely low TSH and falsely high free T4, mimicking Graves disease, and resolves after supplement withdrawal; and heterophilic antibodies or macro-TSH can distort TSH results. Amiodarone, lithium, and iodine load alter thyroid physiology itself. Reference intervals for TSH and free T4 are assay- and population-specific, often trimester-specific in pregnancy; always verify locally.

deepStudy.clinicalSignificance: Diagnostic thresholds determine who is treated: a patient one unit below the fasting glucose cutoff does not have diabetes by criteria, and a single unconfirmed value should not start lifelong therapy. HbA1c interferences are common in hemodialysis, pregnancy, and hemoglobinopathy populations, where glucose-based testing or alternative markers are needed. In thyroid disease, treating an assay artifact (for example biotin-driven pseudothyrotoxicosis) exposes patients to unnecessary antithyroid drugs and even thyroidectomy; a careful supplement history prevents this.
deepStudy.labInterpretation: Report glucose-based results with units and the specimen type (plasma vs whole blood) and method; report HbA1c with the standardization system (NGSP/IFCC) and note known interferences when present. Interpret TSH and free T4 as a pair with the assay-specific reference interval, and comment when interference is suspected (biotin, heterophile antibodies, TBG changes). All reference intervals and diagnostic thresholds vary by laboratory, method, and guideline edition; verify against the performing laboratory and current accepted criteria.

examTraps: HbA1c is not glycosylated hemoglobin measured in some older texts' sense of labile intermediates; it reflects stable ketoamine-linked glycation and is standardized through NGSP/IFCC.
Low TSH with high free T4 can be an artifact of high-dose biotin, not Graves disease; ask about supplements before escalating therapy.
Gestational diabetes protocols differ (one-step 75 g vs two-step 50 g then 100 g); cite the local protocol rather than mixing cutoffs.

memoryHooks.text: The diabetes club: 126 (fasting), 200 (random or OGTT 2-hour), 6.5 (A1c) — and when in doubt, repeat for confirmation.
memoryHooks.funny: 126-200-6.5: parang combo meal ng diabetes diagnosis. Pag walang symptoms, double-check muna — wag padalos-dalos, di ito grab.

memoryHooks.text: Biotin (B7) sneaks into the assay and steals the signal: TSH looks low, free T4 looks high — a fake Graves disease that disappears when the supplement stops.
memoryHooks.funny: Biotin = con artist ng thyroid panel. 'Graves ka daw!' sabi ng machine. Pero supplement lang pala. Kaya mag-tanong lagi: 'Umiinom ka ba ng vitamins?'
